deep.reconstruction:
This page has no calculation. It is a heavily corrected prose draft (pencil) for the historical part, §2, of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (written 1853–54, published 1867). The neighbouring pages fit this. The previous page drafts remarks on the history of the terms 'unendliche Reihe' and 'Convergenz' (Newton, Mercator). The next page is an outline of the sections: d'Alembert, Euler and Daniel Bernoulli; Fourier and Dirichlet; the definition of the definite integral.

Content, reconstructed sentence by sentence.
(1) 'Dirichlet setzt [zwar bei seinem Beweise nur] voraus, dass die Function [durchgehends] endlich und stetig sei.' This refers to Dirichlet's proof (Crelle 4, 1829) that the Fourier series of f converges to (f(x+0)+f(x-0))/2. The proof uses the Dirichlet kernel and the second mean value theorem. In modern terms Dirichlet assumes f is bounded, piecewise continuous and piecewise monotone, i.e. has finitely many maxima and minima.
(2) 'Seine Schlüsse sind aber [selbst] ganz unabhängig davon, ob die Function stetig ist, und [bleiben] selbst giltig, wenn [die Function zwar ... ] unendlich oft [unstetig] ist ...' Riemann observes that the argument does not really need continuity. It survives discontinuities, even infinitely many, provided the integrals involved still make sense.
(3) A struck passage on 'den Fall, wo die Function unendlich wird ... die eine Integration gestattet'. This concerns functions that become unbounded at isolated points but remain (improperly) integrable.
(4) 'Unendlich oft oscilliren können die Function nur an den Grenzen der Integration ..., dieser Fall lässt sich [auf] den Satz [zurückführen].' This is partly struck. It says infinitely many oscillations (infinitely many maxima and minima) are allowed only at the endpoints of the integration intervals, and this case reduces to the theorem.
(5) 'Die Ausdehnung des Satzes auf den Fall, wo die Function unendlich wird, unendlich oft oscillirt und an den Grenzen [unstetig] ist, giebt Dirichlet in einer spätern Note.' The later treatment is most likely Dirichlet 1837, Dove's Repertorium der Physik, 'Über die Darstellung ganz willkürlicher Functionen durch Sinus- und Cosinusreihen'. That paper allows functions that become infinite at finitely many points, provided the integral of f exists.
(6) Reference note: 'Dirichlet in Crelle's Journal.'

The published §2/§3 of the Habilitationsschrift contains the polished version of these remarks. Its point is that Dirichlet's conditions leave open exactly two cases: non-integrable functions, and functions with infinitely many maxima and minima. Riemann then attacks these via his new definition of the integral.

Historically, Dirichlet's 1829 hypotheses were finitely many discontinuities and finitely many maxima and minima, not continuity alone. Riemann's draft wording 'nur voraus, dass die Function endlich und stetig sei' is a compression. The published text states Dirichlet's hypotheses more carefully.

results.what: Assessment of the scope of Dirichlet's 1829 convergence proof for Fourier series: the argument does not need continuity and extends to (improperly) integrable unbounded functions and to infinite oscillation at the interval ends.
results.modern_name: Dirichlet's theorem on pointwise convergence of Fourier series (Dirichlet conditions) and its extensions
results.usually_credited_to: P. G. L. Dirichlet (1829, Crelle 4; extension 1837); the critical survey is credited to Riemann, Habilitationsschrift 1854 (publ. 1867)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of the well-known historical section of Riemann's 1854 Habilitationsschrift on trigonometric series. Its content (Riemann's discussion of what Dirichlet's proof covers) appears in the published text.

Line 3–4 likely reads 'Seine Schlüsse sind aber selbst ganz unabhängig davon, ob die Function stetig ist, und [bleiben] selbst giltig, wenn ... zwar ... unendlich oft unstetig ist'.
